```{python}
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### 51 — cGh cube {#sec-cghcube}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@okun1991fundamental] \
> **Domain:** physical theories placed by their constants

The cGh cube places physical theories at the vertices of a cube whose axes are the constants c, G and h, so each theory is fixed by which constants it takes seriously. Okun popularised the cube as a map of the fundamental theories [@okun1991fundamental].

```{python}
#| label: fig-cghcube
#| fig-cap: "The cube of physical theories: axes 1/c, G, h; each vertex a theory taking those constants seriously."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D  # noqa: F401
import itertools

verts = list(itertools.product([0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1]))
labels = {
    (0, 0, 0): "Newtonian\nmechanics",
    (1, 0, 0): "Special\nrelativity",
    (0, 1, 0): "Newtonian\ngravity",
    (0, 0, 1): "Quantum\nmechanics",
    (1, 1, 0): "General\nrelativity",
    (1, 0, 1): "QFT",
    (0, 1, 1): "Non-rel.\nquantum gravity",
    (1, 1, 1): "Theory of\neverything",
}

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
for a in verts:
    for b in verts:
        if sum(abs(ai - bi) for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) == 1:
            ax.plot(*zip(a, b), color="#9db4e2", lw=1.0)
for v in verts:
    ax.scatter(*v, s=40, color="#ff725c")
    ax.text(v[0], v[1], v[2], "  " + labels[v], fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlabel("1/c"); ax.set_ylabel("G"); ax.set_zlabel("h")
ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_zticks([0, 1])
ax.set_title("The cGh cube of theories")
ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=-55)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### 52 — Standard Model double simplex {#sec-standardmodel}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@workman2022review] \
> **Domain:** particles placed to show interactions

The Standard Model table arranges the fundamental particles as tiles — three generations of quarks and leptons plus the gauge bosons and the Higgs — coloured by kind so the interaction pattern reads off the grid. The Particle Data Group review is the canonical tabulation [@workman2022review].

```{python}
#| label: fig-standardmodel
#| fig-cap: "The Standard Model as a tile chart: quarks and leptons over three generations, with bosons and the Higgs aside."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches

quark, lepton, boson, scalar = "#4269d0", "#6cc5b0", "#efb118", "#a463f2"

# rows top->bottom, columns are generations
rows = [
    [("u", quark), ("c", quark), ("t", quark)],
    [("d", quark), ("s", quark), ("b", quark)],
    [("e", lepton), (u"μ", lepton), (u"τ", lepton)],
    [(u"νₑ", lepton), (u"νμ", lepton), (u"ντ", lepton)],
]
bosons = [("g", boson), (u"γ", boson), ("Z", boson), ("W", boson), ("H", scalar)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))

def tile(x, y, sym, col):
    ax.add_patch(patches.FancyBboxPatch((x, y), 0.9, 0.9,
                 boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", fc=col, ec="white", lw=1.5, alpha=0.9))
    ax.text(x + 0.45, y + 0.45, sym, ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=12, color="white")

for r, row in enumerate(rows):
    for c, (sym, col) in enumerate(row):
        tile(c, len(rows) - 1 - r, sym, col)
for i, (sym, col) in enumerate(bosons):
    tile(4, len(bosons) - 1 - i, sym, col)

for c in range(3):
    ax.text(c + 0.45, 4.15, f"gen {c+1}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax.text(4.45, 5.15, "bosons", ha="center", fontsize=8)

handles = [patches.Patch(color=quark, label="quark"),
           patches.Patch(color=lepton, label="lepton"),
           patches.Patch(color=boson, label="gauge boson"),
           patches.Patch(color=scalar, label="scalar")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, -0.18),
          ncol=4, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 5.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 5.4)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("Standard Model particle tiles")
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### 53 — Cultural history as a network {#sec-culturenet}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@schich2014network] \
> **Domain:** 150,000 lives over two millennia

A cultural-history network draws lives as directed edges from birthplace to death-place between geographic centres, edge weight tracing the migration of talent. Schich and colleagues mapped 150,000 notable lives over two millennia this way [@schich2014network].

```{python}
#| label: fig-culturenet
#| fig-cap: "A birth-to-death migration graph over synthetic cultural centres; arrow width scales with flow."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

centres = {
    "Rome": (12.5, 41.9), "Paris": (2.3, 48.9), "London": (-0.1, 51.5),
    "Vienna": (16.4, 48.2), "Berlin": (13.4, 52.5), "Florence": (11.3, 43.8),
    "Madrid": (-3.7, 40.4), "Amsterdam": (4.9, 52.4),
}
flows = [
    ("Florence", "Rome", 9), ("Rome", "Paris", 6), ("Vienna", "Berlin", 7),
    ("Madrid", "Rome", 4), ("Amsterdam", "London", 5), ("Paris", "London", 6),
    ("Berlin", "Paris", 3), ("Florence", "Vienna", 4), ("London", "Paris", 5),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
for src, dst, w in flows:
    x0, y0 = centres[src]
    x1, y1 = centres[dst]
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#4269d0",
                                lw=0.4 * w, alpha=0.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.15"))
for name, (x, y) in centres.items():
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=90, color="#ff725c", edgecolors="white",
               linewidths=0.6, zorder=3)
    ax.text(x, y + 0.6, name, ha="center", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude"); ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")
ax.set_title("Birth-to-death migration of cultural figures")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## B2. Continuity and flow — directed paths and bands {#sec-unit-b2}

*After Tufte's reading of Minard, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983).*

### 54 — Water & carbon cycle {#sec-carboncycle}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@falkowski2000global] \
> **Domain:** closed-loop flows  

Reservoirs sit as labelled boxes and fluxes run between them as directed arrows whose width scales with the mass moved per year, so a conserved quantity is tracked around a closed loop. Falkowski and colleagues drew the carbon budget in exactly this box-and-flux idiom to weigh the anthropogenic perturbation against the natural cycle [@falkowski2000global].

```{python}
#| label: fig-carboncycle
#| fig-cap: "Carbon reservoirs as boxes, fluxes as arrows with width scaled to magnitude."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))

boxes = {
    "Atmosphere": (0.50, 0.82),
    "Ocean": (0.16, 0.40),
    "Biosphere": (0.84, 0.40),
    "Sediments": (0.50, 0.06),
}
bw, bh = 0.26, 0.15
for name, (x, y) in boxes.items():
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x - bw / 2, y - bh / 2), bw, bh,
                           facecolor="#4269d0", edgecolor="black", alpha=0.85))
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", color="white",
            fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")

# (from, to, GtC/yr)
fluxes = [
    ("Ocean", "Atmosphere", 90),
    ("Atmosphere", "Ocean", 92),
    ("Biosphere", "Atmosphere", 120),
    ("Atmosphere", "Biosphere", 123),
    ("Biosphere", "Sediments", 0.5),
    ("Ocean", "Sediments", 0.2),
]
for src, dst, val in fluxes:
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = boxes[src], boxes[dst]
    dx, dy = x1 - x0, y1 - y0
    n = np.hypot(dx, dy)
    ox, oy = -dy / n * 0.03, dx / n * 0.03  # offset so opposing arrows separate
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1 - dx * 0.28 + ox, y1 - dy * 0.28 + oy),
                xytext=(x0 + dx * 0.28 + ox, y0 + dy * 0.28 + oy),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ff725c",
                                lw=0.6 + 2.2 * np.sqrt(val / 120)))

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Carbon cycle: reservoirs and fluxes (GtC yr$^{-1}$)", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 55 — Trophic / energy-flow pyramid {#sec-trophic}

> **Class:** named first + canonical reference (distinct documents) \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@lindeman1942trophic] \
> **Named first:** [@elton1927animal]  
> **Domain:** energy through an ecosystem  

Stacked tiers taper from a wide base of producers to a narrow apex, each level roughly a tenth of the one below because most energy is lost as heat at every transfer. Elton drew the pyramid of numbers [@elton1927animal]; Lindeman recast it as a quantitative energy budget with the ~10% trophic efficiency [@lindeman1942trophic].

```{python}
#| label: fig-trophic
#| fig-cap: "Trophic pyramid; each tier holds roughly 10% of the energy of the level below."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)

levels = ["Producers", "Primary\nconsumers", "Secondary\nconsumers",
          "Tertiary\nconsumers", "Apex\npredators"]
energy = np.array([10000.0, 1000.0, 100.0, 10.0, 1.0])
widths = energy / energy.max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
colors = ["#3ca951", "#6cc5b0", "#4269d0", "#a463f2", "#ff725c"]
h = 1.0
for i, (w, lab, c) in enumerate(zip(widths, levels, colors)):
    y = i * h
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-w / 2, y), w, h * 0.9, facecolor=c,
                           edgecolor="white"))
    ax.text(0, y + 0.45 * h, f"{lab}\n{energy[i]:.0f}", ha="center",
            va="center", fontsize=7.5,
            color="white" if i != 0 else "black")
    if i > 0:
        ax.annotate("~10%", xy=(w / 2 + 0.03, y + 0.1), fontsize=8,
                    color="0.35")

ax.set_xlim(-0.62, 0.62)
ax.set_ylim(0, len(levels) * h)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Energy pyramid (relative units)", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 56 — Sankey of energy/material flow {#sec-sankey}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@sankey1898thermal] \
> **Domain:** magnitude along paths  

A Sankey diagram splits one input stream into branches whose widths stay proportional to the quantity carried, so conservation and loss are read directly from band thickness. Sankey drew the first such diagram to account for the energy losses of a steam engine [@sankey1898thermal].

```{python}
#| label: fig-sankey
#| fig-cap: "Sankey flow: one input splitting into useful work and two loss streams."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.sankey import Sankey

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 1, 1, xticks=[], yticks=[])

sankey = Sankey(ax=ax, scale=0.6, offset=0.25, head_angle=120, unit=None)
sankey.add(flows=[1.0, -0.52, -0.33, -0.15],
           labels=["input", "useful work", "friction loss", "exhaust"],
           orientations=[0, 0, 1, -1],
           facecolor="#4269d0", edgecolor="#2a2a2a")
diagrams = sankey.finish()

# anchor the horizontal labels clear of their arrowheads
t_in, t_uw, t_fr, t_ex = diagrams[0].texts
t_in.set_ha("right")
t_in.set_position((t_in.get_position()[0] - 0.06, 0.0))
t_uw.set_ha("left")
t_uw.set_position((t_uw.get_position()[0] + 0.02, 0.0))

# widen the frame so every label sits inside it
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
ax.set_xlim(-1.35, 2.15)
ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.35)

ax.set_title("Sankey energy-flow diagram", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 57 — Haber–Bosch / refinery process flow {#sec-processflow}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@bosch1932development] \
> **Domain:** the industrial transformation  

A process-flow diagram chains unit operations as boxes and connects them with directed material streams, closing the loop where unreacted feed is recycled. Bosch described the high-pressure ammonia synthesis this diagram traces — feed compression, catalytic reaction, condensation, and recycle [@bosch1932development].

```{python}
#| label: fig-processflow
#| fig-cap: "Haber–Bosch process flow: feed → compressor → reactor → condenser → product, with recycle."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))

units = {
    "Feed\nN$_2$+H$_2$": (0.10, 0.62),
    "Compressor": (0.34, 0.62),
    "Reactor": (0.58, 0.62),
    "Condenser": (0.82, 0.62),
    "Product\nNH$_3$": (0.82, 0.20),
}
bw, bh = 0.16, 0.16
for name, (x, y) in units.items():
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - bw / 2, y - bh / 2), bw, bh,
                                boxstyle="round,pad=0.01",
                                facecolor="#6cc5b0", edgecolor="black"))
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5)

def arrow(a, b, color="#4269d0"):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = units[a], units[b]
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=1.6,
                                shrinkA=22, shrinkB=22))

arrow("Feed\nN$_2$+H$_2$", "Compressor")
arrow("Compressor", "Reactor")
arrow("Reactor", "Condenser")
arrow("Condenser", "Product\nNH$_3$")

# recycle loop: condenser -> back to compressor
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.34, 0.70), xytext=(0.82, 0.78),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ff725c", lw=1.4,
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.35"))
ax.text(0.58, 0.86, "recycle", ha="center", fontsize=8, color="#ff725c")

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Ammonia synthesis process flow", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 58 — Central dogma {#sec-centraldogma}

> **Class:** named first + canonical reference (distinct documents) \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@crick1970central] \
> **Named first:** [@crick1958protein]  
> **Domain:** directional flow of information  

Information passes DNA → RNA → protein along labelled arrows, with replication looping back onto DNA, and the arrow that is absent — protein back to nucleic acid — is the claim. Crick named the central dogma [@crick1958protein] and restated it precisely a decade later [@crick1970central].

```{python}
#| label: fig-centraldogma
#| fig-cap: "Central dogma: DNA transcribed to RNA, translated to protein; DNA self-replicates."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))

nodes = {"DNA": (0.20, 0.45), "RNA": (0.50, 0.45), "protein": (0.80, 0.45)}
for name, (x, y) in nodes.items():
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.10, facecolor="#4269d0", alpha=0.85,
                        edgecolor="black"))
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", color="white",
            fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")

ax.annotate("", xy=(0.40, 0.45), xytext=(0.30, 0.45),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=1.6))
ax.text(0.35, 0.52, "transcription", ha="center", fontsize=7.5)
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.70, 0.45), xytext=(0.60, 0.45),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=1.6))
ax.text(0.65, 0.52, "translation", ha="center", fontsize=7.5)

# replication self-loop on DNA
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.14, 0.55), xytext=(0.26, 0.55),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ff725c", lw=1.4,
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-1.4"))
ax.text(0.20, 0.74, "replication", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color="#ff725c")

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0.15, 0.85)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("The central dogma of molecular biology", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 59 — Shannon channel + entropy {#sec-shannon}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@shannon1948mathematical] \
> **Domain:** information through noise  

The communication system is drawn as a chain — source, encoder, noisy channel, decoder, destination — and the amount of information is measured by an entropy that peaks when outcomes are equiprobable. Shannon set out both the block diagram and the entropy function in one paper [@shannon1948mathematical].

```{python}
#| label: fig-shannon
#| fig-cap: "Shannon's channel block diagram (left) and binary entropy H(p), maximal at p=0.5 (right)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6, 3.2),
                               gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.25, 1]})

# left: block diagram
blocks = ["Source", "Encoder", "Channel", "Decoder", "Dest."]
ys = np.linspace(0.85, 0.15, len(blocks))
for b, y in zip(blocks, ys):
    ax0.add_patch(Rectangle((0.25, y - 0.06), 0.5, 0.10,
                            facecolor="#4269d0", alpha=0.85, edgecolor="black"))
    ax0.text(0.5, y - 0.01, b, ha="center", va="center", color="white",
             fontsize=8)
for y0, y1 in zip(ys[:-1], ys[1:]):
    ax0.annotate("", xy=(0.5, y1 + 0.04), xytext=(0.5, y0 - 0.06),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=1.3))
ax0.annotate("noise", xy=(0.75, ys[2] - 0.01), xytext=(0.98, ys[2] - 0.01),
             ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8, color="#ff725c",
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ff725c", lw=1.3))
ax0.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax0.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax0.axis("off")
ax0.set_title("Channel", fontsize=10)

# right: binary entropy
p = np.linspace(1e-6, 1 - 1e-6, 400)
H = -p * np.log2(p) - (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p)
ax1.plot(p, H, color="#a463f2", lw=2)
ax1.axvline(0.5, color="0.6", ls="--", lw=1)
ax1.set_xlabel("p")
ax1.set_ylabel("H(p)  bits")
ax1.set_title("Binary entropy", fontsize=10)
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 60 — Greenhouse / energy-balance (Trenberth) diagram {#sec-energybudget}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@trenberth2009earth] \
> **Named first:** [@kiehl1997earth]  
> **Domain:** the energy budget  

Broad arrows carry incoming solar, reflected shortwave, outgoing longwave, and downward back-radiation, each tagged with a global-mean flux in W m⁻², so the planetary balance closes to a small residual. Kiehl and Trenberth fixed the canonical numbers [@kiehl1997earth]; Trenberth, Fasullo, and Kiehl revised them for the modern budget [@trenberth2009earth].

```{python}
#| label: fig-energybudget
#| fig-cap: "Earth's energy budget: solar in, shortwave reflected, longwave out, back-radiation (W m$^{-2}$)."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))

# surface and top-of-atmosphere reference lines
ax.axhline(0.12, color="#6cc5b0", lw=6, alpha=0.5)   # surface
ax.axhline(0.92, color="0.75", lw=2)                 # top of atmosphere
ax.text(0.02, 0.06, "surface", fontsize=8, color="0.35")
ax.text(0.02, 0.95, "top of atmosphere", fontsize=8, color="0.35")

def flux(x, y0, y1, val, color, label, side="left"):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x, y1), xytext=(x, y0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color,
                                lw=1 + val / 90))
    ax.text(x + (0.02 if side == "left" else -0.02), (y0 + y1) / 2,
            f"{label}\n{val}", fontsize=7.5, color=color,
            ha="left" if side == "left" else "right", va="center")

flux(0.16, 0.92, 0.12, 341, "#efb118", "solar in")
flux(0.40, 0.12, 0.92, 102, "#4269d0", "reflected", side="right")
flux(0.64, 0.12, 0.92, 239, "#ff725c", "longwave out")
flux(0.88, 0.55, 0.12, 333, "#9c6b4e", "back-rad.", side="right")

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Earth's energy balance (W m$^{-2}$)", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 61 — Out-of-Africa migration map {#sec-outofafrica}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@cann1987mitochondrial] \
> **Domain:** movement across space  

Arrows radiate from East Africa across an abstracted world, each annotated with an approximate arrival date, turning a genealogy into a route across space and time. Cann, Stoneking, and Wilson's mitochondrial coalescence placed the common ancestor in Africa and set this migration narrative going [@cann1987mitochondrial].

```{python}
#| label: fig-outofafrica
#| fig-cap: "Abstract world map with dispersal arrows from East Africa, dates in thousand years ago."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, facecolor="#eef2f7", edgecolor="none"))

regions = {
    "E. Africa": (0.50, 0.42),
    "Europe": (0.52, 0.72),
    "Asia": (0.72, 0.62),
    "Australia": (0.86, 0.20),
    "Americas": (0.15, 0.55),
}
for name, (x, y) in regions.items():
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=40, color="#3ca951", zorder=3)
    ax.text(x, y + 0.04, name, ha="center", fontsize=7.5)

origin = regions["E. Africa"]
routes = [("Europe", "45 kya"), ("Asia", "50 kya"),
          ("Australia", "50 kya"), ("Americas", "16 kya")]
for dest, date in routes:
    x1, y1 = regions[dest]
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=origin,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ff725c", lw=1.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.2",
                                shrinkA=6, shrinkB=6))
    ax.text((origin[0] + x1) / 2, (origin[1] + y1) / 2 - 0.03, date,
            fontsize=7, color="#ff725c", ha="center")

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Out-of-Africa dispersal", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 62 — Minard's march on Moscow {#sec-minard}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@minard1869carte] \
> **Domain:** six variables, one frame  

A band whose width tracks the surviving army thins along the advance and thins again on the retreat, while a linked panel below plots the falling temperature against longitude — six variables held in one frame. Minard's flow map of Napoleon's 1812 campaign is the canonical instance [@minard1869carte].

```{python}
#| label: fig-minard
#| fig-cap: "Minard idiom: army-size band (advance vs retreat) above, retreat temperature below."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

# hand-entered (longitude, army size in thousands)
adv_lon = np.array([24.0, 26.8, 28.5, 30.2, 33.2, 36.0, 37.6])
adv_size = np.array([340, 300, 280, 240, 180, 145, 100])
ret_lon = np.array([37.6, 36.0, 33.2, 30.2, 28.5, 26.8, 24.0])
ret_size = np.array([100, 90, 55, 40, 30, 20, 10])
ret_temp = np.array([0, -9, -21, -11, -20, -24, -26])  # °C, representative

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 4.2), sharex=True,
                               gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1]})

scale = 6000.0
y_adv, y_ret = 1.0, 0.4
ax0.fill_between(adv_lon, y_adv - adv_size / scale, y_adv + adv_size / scale,
                 color="#c9a227", alpha=0.9, label="advance")
ax0.fill_between(ret_lon, y_ret - ret_size / scale, y_ret + ret_size / scale,
                 color="#5a5a5a", alpha=0.9, label="retreat")
ax0.text(24, y_adv + 0.10, "Kaunas", fontsize=7.5, ha="center")
ax0.text(37.6, y_adv + 0.10, "Moscow", fontsize=7.5, ha="center")
ax0.set_ylim(0.2, 1.3)
ax0.set_yticks([])
ax0.legend(loc="center left", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
ax0.set_title("Napoleon's 1812 campaign (Minard idiom)", fontsize=11)

ax1.plot(ret_lon, ret_temp, "o-", color="#4269d0")
for x, t in zip(ret_lon, ret_temp):
    ax1.annotate(f"{t}°", (x, t), textcoords="offset points",
                 xytext=(0, -10), fontsize=7, ha="center")
ax1.set_ylabel("temp °C", fontsize=8)
ax1.set_xlabel("longitude (°E)")
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## B3. Proximity and similarity — clustering, and how machines see {#sec-unit-b3}

*After Cleveland & McGill on ordered comparison, and Ware on grouping by similarity.*

### 63 — Clustered expression heatmap {#sec-heatmap}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@eisen1998cluster] \
> **Domain:** reorder, and clusters appear  

Permuting the rows and columns of an expression matrix by hierarchical clustering pulls co-regulated genes into contiguous blocks that a random ordering hides. Eisen and colleagues introduced the clustered heatmap with its red–green diverging map for genome-wide expression [@eisen1998cluster].

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "The same genes×conditions matrix: random order (left) vs clustered order (right)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, leaves_list

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

ngenes, nconds = 30, 15
data = rng.normal(0, 0.4, (ngenes, nconds))
gene_grp = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], 10)
cond_grp = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], 5)
for g in range(3):
    data[np.ix_(gene_grp == g, cond_grp == g)] += 2.5

# shuffle rows and columns to hide the block structure
rperm = rng.permutation(ngenes)
cperm = rng.permutation(nconds)
shuffled = data[np.ix_(rperm, cperm)]

# recover order by clustering
ro = leaves_list(linkage(shuffled, method="average"))
co = leaves_list(linkage(shuffled.T, method="average"))
clustered = shuffled[np.ix_(ro, co)]

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6, 3.6))
vmax = np.abs(data).max()
for ax, mat, title in [(ax0, shuffled, "shuffled"),
                       (ax1, clustered, "clustered")]:
    ax.imshow(mat, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlabel("conditions")
ax0.set_ylabel("genes")
fig.suptitle("Reorder and the clusters appear", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 64 — Correlation heatmap / scatter-matrix {#sec-splom}

> **Class:** uncertain attribution \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@chambers1983graphical] \
> **Domain:** relationships at scale  

A scatterplot matrix lays every pairwise plot in a grid so structure and correlation across many variables are scanned at once, off-diagonal cells mirroring about the diagonal. Chambers and colleagues codified the scatterplot matrix as a standard tool of graphical analysis [@chambers1983graphical].

```{python}
#| label: fig-splom
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot matrix of four variables with correlation coefficients on the diagonal."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n = 150
z = rng.normal(size=n)
x1 = z + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)
x2 = 0.8 * z + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n)
x3 = -0.7 * z + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n)
X = np.column_stack([z, x1, x2, x3])
names = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

k = X.shape[1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(k, k, figsize=(6, 3.8))
for i in range(k):
    for j in range(k):
        ax = axes[i, j]
        if i == j:
            ax.text(0.5, 0.5, names[i], ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", transform=ax.transAxes)
        elif i > j:
            ax.scatter(X[:, j], X[:, i], s=5, color="#4269d0", alpha=0.5)
        else:
            r = np.corrcoef(X[:, j], X[:, i])[0, 1]
            ax.text(0.5, 0.5, f"{r:+.2f}", ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=10, transform=ax.transAxes,
                    color="#ff725c" if r < 0 else "#3ca951")
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])

fig.suptitle("Scatterplot matrix (SPLOM)", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 65 — Cosine similarity {#sec-cosine}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@salton1975vector] \
> **Domain:** the angle between vectors  

Documents become vectors and their similarity is the cosine of the angle between them, so length drops out and only direction — shared term profile — counts. Salton's vector space model made cosine similarity the standard measure for information retrieval [@salton1975vector].

```{python}
#| label: fig-cosine
#| fig-cap: "Document vectors from the origin; the angle between two gives cosine similarity."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

docs = {"d1": np.array([3.0, 1.0]),
        "d2": np.array([2.5, 2.0]),
        "d3": np.array([0.6, 3.0])}
colors = {"d1": "#4269d0", "d2": "#ff725c", "d3": "#3ca951"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for name, v in docs.items():
    ax.annotate("", xy=v, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=colors[name], lw=2))
    ax.text(v[0] + 0.05, v[1] + 0.05, name, fontsize=9, color=colors[name])

a, b = docs["d1"], docs["d2"]
cos = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
th = np.linspace(np.arctan2(a[1], a[0]), np.arctan2(b[1], b[0]), 30)
ax.plot(0.9 * np.cos(th), 0.9 * np.sin(th), color="0.4", lw=1)
ax.text(1.15, 0.55, f"cos θ = {cos:.2f}", fontsize=9, color="0.3")

ax.set_xlim(0, 3.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 3.4)
ax.set_xlabel("term 1")
ax.set_ylabel("term 2")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("Cosine similarity", fontsize=11)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 66 — t-SNE / UMAP projection {#sec-tsne}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@vandermaaten2008visualizing] \
> **Domain:** high dimensions flattened to 2D  

A nonlinear embedding places high-dimensional points on the plane so that neighbours stay near and distinct groups fall into separated islands. van der Maaten and Hinton introduced t-SNE, whose crisply separated clusters became the signature look of embedding plots [@vandermaaten2008visualizing].

```{python}
#| label: fig-tsne
#| fig-cap: "A 2D embedding: well-separated coloured clusters (simulated t-SNE output)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

centers = np.array([[-6, -5], [5, -4], [0, 6], [7, 5], [-5, 5]])
colors = ["#4269d0", "#efb118", "#ff725c", "#6cc5b0", "#a463f2"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for c, col in zip(centers, colors):
    pts = rng.normal(c, 1.1, size=(60, 2))
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=12, color=col, alpha=0.8)

ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("dim 1")
ax.set_ylabel("dim 2")
ax.set_title("t-SNE / UMAP embedding", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 67 — Word embeddings {#sec-embeddings}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@mikolov2013efficient] \
> **Domain:** semantics as geometry  

Words map to vectors whose differences encode relations, so an analogy becomes a parallelogram: king − man + woman lands near queen. Mikolov and colleagues' word2vec produced these linear analogy structures [@mikolov2013efficient].

```{python}
#| label: fig-embeddings
#| fig-cap: "Word vectors forming the analogy parallelogram king − man + woman ≈ queen."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

words = {"man": np.array([1.0, 1.0]),
         "woman": np.array([3.0, 1.2]),
         "king": np.array([1.3, 3.0]),
         "queen": np.array([3.3, 3.2])}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for w, p in words.items():
    ax.scatter(*p, s=60, color="#4269d0", zorder=3)
    ax.text(p[0] + 0.06, p[1] + 0.06, w, fontsize=10)

def arr(a, b, color):
    ax.annotate("", xy=words[b], xytext=words[a],
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=1.8))

arr("man", "king", "#ff725c")
arr("woman", "queen", "#ff725c")
arr("man", "woman", "#3ca951")
arr("king", "queen", "#3ca951")

ax.set_xlim(0.5, 4.0)
ax.set_ylim(0.5, 3.8)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Word-embedding analogy", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 68 — Art embedding map {#sec-artmap}

> **Class:** uncertain attribution \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@karayev2014recognizing] \
> **Domain:** a collection placed by visual similarity  

Every artwork becomes a point in a plane and visual style pulls similar works together, so a collection self-organises into style neighbourhoods. Karayev and colleagues learned image-style features whose embeddings cluster paintings and photographs by their look [@karayev2014recognizing].

```{python}
#| label: fig-artmap
#| fig-cap: "Artworks embedded in 2D, clustering by visual style (colour = style label)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

styles = ["Impressionist", "Baroque", "Cubist", "Ukiyo-e"]
centers = np.array([[-4, 3], [4, 4], [-3, -4], [5, -3]])
colors = ["#4269d0", "#efb118", "#ff725c", "#6cc5b0"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for name, c, col in zip(styles, centers, colors):
    pts = rng.normal(c, 1.4, size=(40, 2))
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=14, color=col, alpha=0.75, label=name)
    ax.text(c[0], c[1] + 2.0, name, ha="center", fontsize=8, color=col)

ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Art collection by visual style", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower center", ncol=2, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 69 — Stylometry / Burrows's Delta {#sec-delta}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@burrows2002delta] \
> **Domain:** authorship as distance in style-space  

Each text becomes a vector of z-scored frequencies of common words, and the mean absolute difference between two such vectors — Delta — clusters texts by author. Burrows defined the Delta measure for authorship attribution [@burrows2002delta].

```{python}
#| label: fig-delta
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise Burrows's Delta between texts; the author blocks sit on the diagonal."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n_auth, per, n_words = 4, 3, 40
labels, vecs = [], []
for a in range(n_auth):
    signature = rng.normal(0, 1, n_words)  # author's stylistic fingerprint
    for t in range(per):
        vecs.append(signature + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n_words))
        labels.append(f"A{a+1}")
vecs = np.array(vecs)

# z-score each word column across the corpus, then Delta = mean |Δz|
z = (vecs - vecs.mean(0)) / vecs.std(0)
m = len(z)
delta = np.zeros((m, m))
for i in range(m):
    for j in range(m):
        delta[i, j] = np.abs(z[i] - z[j]).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
im = ax.imshow(delta, cmap="viridis")
ax.set_xticks(range(m))
ax.set_yticks(range(m))
ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=7)
ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=7)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Delta distance", fraction=0.046)
ax.set_title("Burrows's Delta between texts", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 70 — Topic model (LDA) {#sec-lda}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@blei2003latent] \
> **Domain:** latent themes as a reduced basis  

Latent Dirichlet allocation represents each document as a mixture over a few latent topics, so a stacked bar reads off how much of every theme a document holds. Blei, Ng, and Jordan introduced LDA and its document-as-topic-mixture representation [@blei2003latent].

```{python}
#| label: fig-lda
#| fig-cap: "Documents as topic mixtures; each stacked bar sums to one over the latent topics."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n_docs, n_topics = 12, 4
mix = rng.dirichlet(alpha=[0.5] * n_topics, size=n_docs)
topics = ["climate", "finance", "biology", "politics"]
colors = ["#4269d0", "#efb118", "#ff725c", "#6cc5b0"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
bottom = np.zeros(n_docs)
x = np.arange(n_docs)
for k in range(n_topics):
    ax.bar(x, mix[:, k], bottom=bottom, color=colors[k], label=topics[k])
    bottom += mix[:, k]

ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"d{i+1}" for i in range(n_docs)], fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("topic proportion")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_title("LDA document–topic mixtures", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=4, loc="upper center",
          bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.12), frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 71 — Emotional arcs of stories {#sec-arcs}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@reagan2016emotional] \
> **Domain:** six narrative shapes from SVD  

Tracking sentiment across narrative time yields a small set of recurring shapes — steady rise, fall-then-rise, rise-then-fall — that a singular value decomposition of many stories reduces to a handful of archetypes. Reagan and colleagues extracted six such emotional arcs from thousands of texts [@reagan2016emotional].

```{python}
#| label: fig-arcs
#| fig-cap: "Three archetypal emotional arcs: rags to riches, man in a hole, Icarus."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
rags = -1.0 + 2.0 * t                                  # rising
hole = 1.0 - 3.0 * np.exp(-((t - 0.5) / 0.22) ** 2)    # down then up
icarus = 1.4 * np.exp(-((t - 0.5) / 0.28) ** 2) - 0.4  # up then down

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(t, rags, color="#4269d0", lw=2, label="rags to riches")
ax.plot(t, hole, color="#ff725c", lw=2, label="man in a hole")
ax.plot(t, icarus, color="#3ca951", lw=2, label="Icarus")
ax.axhline(0, color="0.7", lw=0.8)

ax.set_xlabel("narrative time")
ax.set_ylabel("sentiment")
ax.set_title("Emotional arcs of stories", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## B4. Enclosure, maps, and spatial reasoning {#sec-unit-b4}

*After Bertin on maps and Cairo, The Truthful Art (2016).*

### 72 — Periodic table {#sec-periodic}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@mendeleev1869beziehungen] \
> **Domain:** periodicity by atomic number

A tiled grid indexed by group and period turns the chemistry of an element into a position, and neighbours in a column share properties. Mendeleev arranged the known elements so that the periodic recurrence fell into columns and left gaps for elements not yet found [@mendeleev1869beziehungen].

```{python}
#| label: fig-periodic
#| fig-cap: "The periodic grid: tiles at (group, period), coloured by element category."
```

### 73 — Origin-of-the-elements table {#sec-nucleosynthesis}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@burbidge1957synthesis] \
> **Domain:** the grid recoloured by process

The same tiled grid, recoloured by where each nucleus is forged, turns the table into a map of cosmic history — hydrogen from the Big Bang, iron from exploding stars, the heaviest nuclei from merging neutron stars. Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler, and Hoyle set out the stellar processes that build the elements beyond hydrogen and helium [@burbidge1957synthesis].

```{python}

    "dying low-mass stars": "#efb118",
    "exploding massive stars": "#ff725c",
    "exploding white dwarfs": "#a463f2",
    "merging neutron stars": "#3ca951",
}


def origin(sym):
    if sym in big_bang:
        return "Big Bang"
    if sym in cosmic:
        return "cosmic-ray fission"
    if sym in low_mass:
        return "dying low-mass stars"
    if sym in white_dwarf:
        return "exploding white dwarfs"
    if sym in neutron:
        return "merging neutron stars"
    return "exploding massive stars"

                           facecolor=origin_color[origin(sym)],

    ax.text(g, -p, sym, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color="black")

for i, sym in enumerate(actin):

          ncol=3, fontsize=7, frameon=False)

plt.show()
```
