### 74 — Genetic code wheel {#sec-codonwheel}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@nirenberg1961dependence] \
> **Domain:** codon to amino acid

Three concentric rings — first, second, third base — read from centre outward resolve each of the 64 codons to one amino acid, with synonymous codons falling into the same wedge. Nirenberg and Matthaei cracked the first codon by showing that a poly-uracil template directs synthesis of phenylalanine [@nirenberg1961dependence].

```{python}
#| label: fig-codonwheel
#| fig-cap: "Codon wheel: rings for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd base map 64 codons to amino acids."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

np.random.seed(0)

bases = ["U", "C", "A", "G"]
table = {
    "UU": ("Phe", "Phe", "Leu", "Leu"), "UC": ("Ser",) * 4,
    "UA": ("Tyr", "Tyr", "Stop", "Stop"), "UG": ("Cys", "Cys", "Stop", "Trp"),
    "CU": ("Leu",) * 4, "CC": ("Pro",) * 4,
    "CA": ("His", "His", "Gln", "Gln"), "CG": ("Arg",) * 4,
    "AU": ("Ile", "Ile", "Ile", "Met"), "AC": ("Thr",) * 4,
    "AA": ("Asn", "Asn", "Lys", "Lys"), "AG": ("Ser", "Ser", "Arg", "Arg"),
    "GU": ("Val",) * 4, "GC": ("Ala",) * 4,
    "GA": ("Asp", "Asp", "Glu", "Glu"), "GG": ("Gly",) * 4,
}
one = {"Phe": "F", "Leu": "L", "Ile": "I", "Met": "M", "Val": "V", "Ser": "S",
       "Pro": "P", "Thr": "T", "Ala": "A", "Tyr": "Y", "His": "H", "Gln": "Q",
       "Asn": "N", "Lys": "K", "Asp": "D", "Glu": "E", "Cys": "C", "Trp": "W",
       "Arg": "R", "Gly": "G", "Stop": "*"}
klass = {}
for a in ["Phe", "Leu", "Ile", "Met", "Val", "Ala", "Gly", "Pro", "Trp"]:
    klass[a] = "nonpolar"
for a in ["Ser", "Thr", "Tyr", "Cys", "Asn", "Gln"]:
    klass[a] = "polar"
for a in ["Asp", "Glu"]:
    klass[a] = "acidic"
for a in ["His", "Lys", "Arg"]:
    klass[a] = "basic"
klass["Stop"] = "stop"
class_color = {"nonpolar": "#4269d0", "polar": "#6cc5b0", "acidic": "#ff725c",
               "basic": "#efb118", "stop": "#97737b"}

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 7))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="polar")
ax.set_theta_zero_location("N")
ax.set_theta_direction(-1)
full = 2 * np.pi

for i, b1 in enumerate(bases):
    c = (i + 0.5) * full / 4
    ax.bar(c, 1.0, width=full / 4, bottom=0.0, color="#dfe6f2",
           edgecolor="white", lw=1.0)
    ax.text(c, 0.5, b1, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    for j, b2 in enumerate(bases):
        c2 = (i * 4 + j + 0.5) * full / 16
        ax.bar(c2, 1.0, width=full / 16, bottom=1.0, color="#eef1f7",
               edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
        ax.text(c2, 1.5, b2, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
        aas = table[b1 + b2]
        for k, b3 in enumerate(bases):
            aa = aas[k]
            c3 = (i * 16 + j * 4 + k + 0.5) * full / 64
            ax.bar(c3, 1.0, width=full / 64, bottom=2.0,
                   color=class_color[klass[aa]], edgecolor="white",
                   lw=0.4, alpha=0.9)
            ax.text(c3, 3.35, one[aa], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6)

ax.set_ylim(0, 3.7)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Genetic code wheel", fontsize=12, pad=12)
handles = [Patch(facecolor=v, label=k) for k, v in class_color.items()]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02),
          ncol=5, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 75 — Leontief input–output matrix {#sec-leontief}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@leontief1936quantitative] \
> **Domain:** an economy as a matrix

Laying every sector along both axes and filling cell (i, j) with the flow of output from sector i into sector j renders a whole economy as one matrix, its diagonal thick with intra-industry use. Leontief built the first such input–output table for the United States and solved it as a linear system [@leontief1936quantitative].

```{python}
#| label: fig-leontief
#| fig-cap: "Inter-industry flow matrix: value flowing from row sector to column sector."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

sectors = ["Agriculture", "Mining", "Manufacturing", "Energy",
           "Construction", "Transport", "Services"]
n = len(sectors)
flow = rng.uniform(2, 20, size=(n, n))
flow += np.diag(rng.uniform(40, 90, size=n))  # heavy intra-industry diagonal
flow[2, :] += 15  # manufacturing feeds many
flow = np.round(flow, 0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
im = ax.imshow(flow, cmap="viridis")
ax.set_xticks(range(n))
ax.set_yticks(range(n))
ax.set_xticklabels(sectors, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticklabels(sectors, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("to sector")
ax.set_ylabel("from sector")

for (i, j) in [(0, 0), (2, 2), (2, 4), (5, 6), (6, 6)]:
    ax.text(j, i, f"{flow[i, j]:.0f}", ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=8, color="white", fontweight="bold")

ax.set_title("Leontief input–output matrix", fontsize=11)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="flow")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 76 — Planetary interior cross-sections {#sec-planetinterior}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@dziewonski1981preliminary] \
> **Domain:** layered structure

Concentric shells drawn to scale expose a planet's radial structure — a solid inner core, a liquid outer core, the mantle, and a thin crust — with the density jumping at each boundary. Dziewonski and Anderson fixed the reference radii and densities of Earth's layers in the Preliminary Reference Earth Model [@dziewonski1981preliminary].

```{python}
#| label: fig-planetinterior
#| fig-cap: "Earth's layers to scale (left) and a PREM-style density profile (right)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle

np.random.seed(0)

layers = [
    ("crust", 6371, "#efb118"),
    ("mantle", 6346, "#ff725c"),
    ("outer core", 3480, "#4269d0"),
    ("inner core", 1221, "#6cc5b0"),
]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 4.2))

for name, r, col in layers:  # largest first
    ax1.add_patch(Circle((0, 0), r, facecolor=col, edgecolor="white", lw=1.2))
mids = [(6371 + 6346) / 2, (6346 + 3480) / 2, (3480 + 1221) / 2, 1221 / 2]
for (name, _, _), m in zip(layers, mids):
    ax1.annotate(name, xy=(0, m), xytext=(6900, m - 200 + 900 * (name == "crust")),
                 fontsize=8, ha="left", va="center",
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="0.4", lw=0.8))
ax1.set_xlim(-6800, 11500)
ax1.set_ylim(-6800, 6800)
ax1.set_aspect("equal")
ax1.axis("off")
ax1.set_title("Cross-section", fontsize=11)

r = np.linspace(0, 6371, 700)
rho = np.piecewise(
    r,
    [r < 1221, (r >= 1221) & (r < 3480), (r >= 3480) & (r < 5701),
     (r >= 5701) & (r < 6346), r >= 6346],
    [lambda r: 13.0 - 0.00016 * r,
     lambda r: 12.2 - 0.001 * (r - 1221),
     lambda r: 5.6 - 0.00053 * (r - 3480),
     lambda r: 4.0 - 0.00108 * (r - 5701),
     lambda r: 2.9],
)
ax2.plot(r, rho, color="#4269d0", lw=2)
for _, b, _ in layers[1:]:
    ax2.axvline(b, color="0.7", ls="--", lw=0.8)
ax2.set_xlabel("radius (km)")
ax2.set_ylabel("density (g/cm$^3$)")
ax2.set_title("PREM density profile", fontsize=11)
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 77 — Biogeography map / Wallace line {#sec-wallace}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@wallace1876geographical] \
> **Domain:** boundaries in space

A single line drawn between adjacent islands can separate two faunas that never mixed, making a deep-water barrier legible as a border on the map. Wallace traced the sharp zoological divide running between Bali and Lombok that splits Asian from Australian animals [@wallace1876geographical].

```{python}
#| label: fig-wallace
#| fig-cap: "Schematic map: the Wallace Line dividing Asian (Sunda) from Australian (Sahul) fauna."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))

asian_is = [(1.6, 3.2, 2.0, 1.1), (2.4, 1.4, 1.5, 0.9),
            (3.4, 3.7, 1.1, 0.7), (3.6, 2.0, 0.9, 0.6)]
aus_is = [(7.6, 2.1, 2.4, 1.6), (6.7, 3.7, 1.2, 0.7), (8.4, 3.8, 0.9, 0.6)]
for (x, y, w, h) in asian_is:
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), w, h, facecolor="#cfe0b8", edgecolor="0.5", lw=0.8))
for (x, y, w, h) in aus_is:
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), w, h, facecolor="#e0cdb0", edgecolor="0.5", lw=0.8))

# Wallace Line
ax.plot([4.7, 5.3], [0.2, 4.8], color="#ff725c", lw=2.5, ls="--")
ax.text(4.6, 4.9, "Wallace Line", color="#ff725c", fontsize=9, ha="right")

# fauna points, coloured by region
for (x, y, w, h) in asian_is:
    pts = rng.normal([x, y], [w / 3, h / 3], size=(9, 2))
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=22, color="#4269d0", zorder=3)
for (x, y, w, h) in aus_is:
    pts = rng.normal([x, y], [w / 3, h / 3], size=(9, 2))
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=22, color="#efb118", marker="^", zorder=3)

ax.scatter([], [], color="#4269d0", label="Asian fauna (Sunda)")
ax.scatter([], [], color="#efb118", marker="^", label="Australian fauna (Sahul)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 5.2)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Wallace's biogeographic boundary", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=8, frameon=False, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 78 — John Snow's cholera map {#sec-snow}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@snow1855mode] \
> **Domain:** spatial pattern as causal argument

Plotting each death as a dot turns a street into an argument: the cases pile up around one water pump and thin with distance from it, so the spatial pattern itself names the cause. Snow mapped the 1854 Soho outbreak and traced it to the Broad Street pump [@snow1855mode] — the second beat of the Day-One pairing, where a map, not a table, carries the inference.

```{python}
#| label: fig-snow
#| fig-cap: "Dot map of cholera deaths clustered on the Broad Street pump."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

broad = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
pumps = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [3.2, 1.6], [-2.9, 2.1],
                  [1.6, -3.1], [-3.1, -2.4], [3.6, -1.8]])

deaths = rng.normal(broad, 0.95, size=(190, 2))
scatter = rng.uniform(-4.2, 4.2, size=(28, 2))
alld = np.vstack([deaths, scatter])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
ax.scatter(alld[:, 0], alld[:, 1], s=14, color="#333333", alpha=0.7, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(pumps[1:, 0], pumps[1:, 1], marker="s", s=90, color="#4269d0",
           edgecolor="white", zorder=3, label="other pumps")
ax.scatter(*broad, marker="s", s=160, color="#ff725c", edgecolor="black",
           zorder=4, label="Broad Street pump")
ax.text(0.2, 0.35, "Broad St", fontsize=8, color="#ff725c")

ax.set_xlim(-5, 5)
ax.set_ylim(-5, 5)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Snow's cholera map", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 79 — Gerrymander / districting {#sec-gerrymander}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@griffith1907rise] \
> **Domain:** how boundaries manufacture outcomes

Holding the votes fixed and redrawing the district lines changes who wins, so the partition — not the electorate — sets the seat count. Griffith gave the first systematic geometric analysis of how district shape converts votes into representation [@griffith1907rise].

```{python}
#| label: fig-gerrymander
#| fig-cap: "Same 60/40 grid, two partitions: 3–2 by columns versus 5–0 by rows."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)

grid = np.zeros((5, 5), int)
grid[:, 3:] = 1  # columns 0-2 party A, columns 3-4 party B  -> 60/40
colors = {0: "#4269d0", 1: "#efb118"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 4.4))


def draw(ax, title):
    for i in range(5):
        for j in range(5):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j, 4 - i), 1, 1, facecolor=colors[grid[i, j]],
                                   edgecolor="white", lw=1.0))
    ax.set_xlim(0, 5)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)


# Panel 1: districts = columns -> A wins 3, B wins 2
draw(axes[0], "Districts by column:  A 3 – B 2")
for j in range(1, 5):
    axes[0].plot([j, j], [0, 5], color="black", lw=2.5)

# Panel 2: districts = rows -> each row 3A/2B -> A wins 5, B wins 0
draw(axes[1], "Districts by row:  A 5 – B 0")
for i in range(1, 5):
    axes[1].plot([0, 5], [i, i], color="black", lw=2.5)

fig.suptitle("Same votes, different maps", fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 80 — Minkowski / light cone {#sec-lightcone}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@minkowski1909raum] \
> **Domain:** the cone partitions spacetime

Drawing space against time and marking the 45° paths of light carves spacetime into a causal future, a causal past, and an unreachable "elsewhere". Minkowski recast special relativity as geometry on this four-dimensional continuum, with the cone dividing what an event can and cannot influence [@minkowski1909raum].

```{python}
#| label: fig-lightcone
#| fig-cap: "A spacetime diagram: light cones partition future, past, and spacelike elsewhere."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

lim = 4.0
x = np.linspace(-lim, lim, 200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5.6))

# timelike future and past (|ct| > |x|)
ax.fill_between(x, np.abs(x), lim, color="#4269d0", alpha=0.18)
ax.fill_between(x, -lim, -np.abs(x), color="#ff725c", alpha=0.18)
# spacelike elsewhere (|x| > |ct|)
ax.fill_betweenx(x, np.abs(x), lim, color="0.85")
ax.fill_betweenx(x, -lim, -np.abs(x), color="0.85")

ax.plot(x, x, color="black", lw=1.5)
ax.plot(x, -x, color="black", lw=1.5)

# a worldline through the origin, staying timelike
ct = np.linspace(-lim, lim, 100)
wl = 0.35 * ct + 0.15 * np.sin(ct)
ax.plot(wl, ct, color="#3ca951", lw=2, label="worldline")

ax.text(0, 3.1, "future", ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#26418f")
ax.text(0, -3.3, "past", ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#a3341f")
ax.text(3.0, 0, "elsewhere", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="0.4")
ax.text(-3.0, 0, "elsewhere", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="0.4")

ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim)
ax.set_ylim(-lim, lim)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("ct")
ax.set_title("Minkowski light cone", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 81 — Map projection problem {#sec-projection}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@tissot1881memoire] \
> **Domain:** every map distorts

No flat map preserves both shape and area; placing a small circle at each graticule node makes the distortion visible as the circles swell or stretch toward the poles. Tissot formalised this indicatrix as the general measure of a projection's local error [@tissot1881memoire] — the same tension the AIATSIS prelude raised, that no single frame renders the whole faithfully.

```{python}
#| label: fig-projection
#| fig-cap: "Tissot indicatrices under equirectangular (stretched) and Mercator (inflated) projections."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

np.random.seed(0)

lats = np.arange(-60, 61, 30)
lons = np.arange(-120, 121, 60)
base = 7.0

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.2))


def merc(la):
    return np.degrees(np.log(np.tan(np.pi / 4 + np.radians(la) / 2)))


# Equirectangular: circles become ellipses widening east-west toward poles
for la in np.arange(-90, 91, 30):
    ax1.axhline(la, color="0.85", lw=0.7)
for lo in np.arange(-180, 181, 60):
    ax1.axvline(lo, color="0.85", lw=0.7)
for la in lats:
    for lo in lons:
        w = base / np.cos(np.radians(la))
        ax1.add_patch(Ellipse((lo, la), w, base, facecolor="#4269d0",
                              alpha=0.5, edgecolor="#26418f"))
ax1.set_xlim(-180, 180)
ax1.set_ylim(-90, 90)
ax1.set_aspect("equal")
ax1.set_title("Equirectangular", fontsize=11)
ax1.set_xlabel("longitude")
ax1.set_ylabel("latitude")

# Mercator: circles stay circles but inflate toward poles
for la in np.arange(-75, 76, 30):
    ax2.axhline(merc(la), color="0.85", lw=0.7)
for lo in np.arange(-180, 181, 60):
    ax2.axvline(lo, color="0.85", lw=0.7)
for la in lats:
    for lo in lons:
        r = base / np.cos(np.radians(la))
        ax2.add_patch(Ellipse((lo, merc(la)), r, r, facecolor="#ff725c",
                              alpha=0.5, edgecolor="#a3341f"))
ax2.set_xlim(-180, 180)
ax2.set_ylim(merc(-78), merc(78))
ax2.set_aspect("equal")
ax2.set_title("Mercator", fontsize=11)
ax2.set_xlabel("longitude")
ax2.set_ylabel("projected y")

fig.suptitle("Every projection distorts", fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## B5. Closure, common fate, and the diagnostic pattern {#sec-unit-b5}

*After Ware on Gestalt closure and common fate (2004).*

### 82 — Blackbody curve + spectral lines {#sec-blackbody}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@planck1901gesetz] \
> **Domain:** lines pop against the continuum

The smooth Planck continuum sets the backdrop against which sharp absorption lines read as notches — closure fills the missing light, so the eye completes the curve and the dark lines stand out. Planck derived the radiance law by quantising the oscillators of the cavity wall [@planck1901gesetz], and its peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as temperature climbs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-blackbody
#| fig-cap: "Planck curves at three temperatures; absorption lines notched into the hottest."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

h, c, kB = 6.626e-34, 2.998e8, 1.381e-23
lam = np.linspace(100e-9, 2000e-9, 800)


def planck(lam, T):
    return 2 * h * c**2 / lam**5 / (np.exp(h * c / (lam * kB * T)) - 1)


colors = {4000: "#ff725c", 5000: "#efb118", 6000: "#4269d0"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
for T, col in colors.items():
    B = planck(lam, T)
    if T == 6000:  # notch a few Fraunhofer-style absorption lines
        for line in [430e-9, 589e-9, 656e-9]:
            B = B * (1 - 0.55 * np.exp(-((lam - line) / 4e-9) ** 2))
    ax.plot(lam * 1e9, B / 1e13, color=col, lw=1.8, label=f"{T} K")

ax.set_xlabel("wavelength (nm)")
ax.set_ylabel("spectral radiance (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Blackbody continuum with absorption lines", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 83 — CMB angular power spectrum {#sec-cmbspectrum}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@debernardis2000flat] \
> **Domain:** the acoustic peaks

Power plotted against multipole rises to a first acoustic peak near ℓ ≈ 200 and then rings down in damped harmonics — a single wave train the eye groups by common fate. The BOOMERANG flight resolved that first peak and pinned the geometry of the universe to flat [@debernardis2000flat].

```{python}
#| label: fig-cmbspectrum
#| fig-cap: "Synthesised CMB angular power spectrum with acoustic peaks and Silk damping."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

ell = np.arange(2, 2500)
plateau = 900 * (1 - np.exp(-ell / 45))
damping = np.exp(-(ell / 1400) ** 2)
acoustic = 5200 * damping * (0.5 + 0.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (ell - 220) / 300))
D = 0.45 * plateau + acoustic

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.plot(ell, D, color="#4269d0", lw=2)
ax.axvline(220, color="0.7", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(232, D.max() * 0.9, r"first peak $\ell\approx220$", fontsize=8, color="0.4")

ax.set_xlabel(r"multipole moment  $\ell$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\ell(\ell+1)C_\ell/2\pi$  ($\mu$K$^2$)")
ax.set_title("CMB angular power spectrum", fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(2, 2400)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 84 — Higgs discovery bump {#sec-higgs}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@aad2012observation] \
> **Domain:** a particle as a bump

A new particle announces itself as a small Gaussian bump riding on a smooth falling background in the invariant-mass spectrum; closure separates the excess from the continuum the eye extrapolates beneath it. The ATLAS collaboration reported such an excess near 125 GeV, the signature of the Higgs boson [@aad2012observation].

```{python}
#| label: fig-higgs
#| fig-cap: "Diphoton invariant-mass spectrum: a small bump near 125 GeV over a falling background."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

edges = np.linspace(100, 160, 31)
m = 0.5 * (edges[:-1] + edges[1:])
background = 6000 * np.exp(-(m - 100) / 22)
signal = 320 * np.exp(-(m - 125) ** 2 / (2 * 2.0 ** 2))
expected = background + signal
data = rng.poisson(expected)
err = np.sqrt(data)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.errorbar(m, data, yerr=err, fmt="o", ms=4, color="#333333",
            capsize=2, label="data")
ax.plot(m, background, color="#ff725c", lw=1.8, ls="--", label="background fit")
ax.plot(m, expected, color="#4269d0", lw=1.8, label="background + signal")

ax.set_xlabel("diphoton invariant mass $m_{\\gamma\\gamma}$ (GeV)")
ax.set_ylabel("events / 2 GeV")
ax.set_title("A resonance at 125 GeV", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 85 — Double-slit interference {#sec-doubleslit}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@young1804bakerian] \
> **Domain:** the wave pattern itself

Two slits produce a cosine fringe pattern modulated by a single-slit envelope, and the regular banding is read as one continuous wave field. Young's Bakerian lecture argued from exactly this pattern that light interferes, and so behaves as a wave [@young1804bakerian].

```{python}
#| label: fig-doubleslit
#| fig-cap: "Two-slit intensity under a single-slit envelope, with the fringe strip below."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

x = np.linspace(-0.03, 0.03, 1200)
lam, d, a, L = 600e-9, 40e-6, 8e-6, 1.0
alpha = np.pi * d * x / (lam * L)
beta = np.pi * a * x / (lam * L)
envelope = np.sinc(beta / np.pi) ** 2
intensity = np.cos(alpha) ** 2 * envelope

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 4.2),
                               gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1]})
ax1.plot(x * 1e3, intensity, color="#4269d0", lw=1.4)
ax1.plot(x * 1e3, envelope, color="#ff725c", lw=1.2, ls="--", label="single-slit envelope")
ax1.set_ylabel("intensity")
ax1.set_title("Two-slit interference", fontsize=11)
ax1.legend(fontsize=8)
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

strip = np.tile(intensity, (60, 1))
ax2.imshow(strip, aspect="auto", cmap="gray",
           extent=[x[0] * 1e3, x[-1] * 1e3, 0, 1])
ax2.set_yticks([])
ax2.set_xlabel("screen position (mm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 86 — Fourier decomposition + spectrogram {#sec-fourier}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@fourier1822theorie] \
> **Domain:** signal as frequency

A tangled time signal resolves into a handful of sharp lines once redrawn against frequency, each peak a sinusoidal component the ear and eye recover as one tone. Fourier proved that any such signal decomposes into a sum of sines and cosines [@fourier1822theorie].

```{python}
#| label: fig-fourier
#| fig-cap: "A signal built from three sines (top) and its frequency spectrum (bottom)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

fs = 1000
t = np.linspace(0, 1, fs, endpoint=False)
freqs = [(5, 1.0), (12, 0.6), (20, 0.3)]
signal = sum(a * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t) for f, a in freqs)

spectrum = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(signal)) / (len(t) / 2)
fax = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(t), 1 / fs)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
ax1.plot(t, signal, color="#4269d0", lw=1.2)
ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax1.set_ylabel("amplitude")
ax1.set_title("Signal in time", fontsize=11)
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

ax2.stem(fax, spectrum, basefmt=" ", linefmt="#ff725c", markerfmt="o")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 40)
ax2.set_xlabel("frequency (Hz)")
ax2.set_ylabel("magnitude")
ax2.set_title("Spectrum", fontsize=11)
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 87 — Plate tectonics + seafloor-age stripes {#sec-seafloor}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@vine1963magnetic] \
> **Domain:** the symmetric stripes as one pattern

Magnetic anomalies recorded in new crust form a barcode of normal and reversed stripes that mirrors exactly across the ridge axis, and the symmetry reads as a single pattern generated by spreading. Vine and Matthews argued that these matched stripes record seafloor spreading writing the field's reversals into the rock [@vine1963magnetic].

```{python}
#| label: fig-seafloor
#| fig-cap: "Magnetic stripes mirrored about a mid-ocean ridge, with seafloor age increasing outward."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

dist = np.linspace(0, 200, 600)  # km from ridge axis
bounds = np.array([10, 25, 33, 50, 62, 78, 95, 110, 130, 150, 175])
pol_right = np.where(np.searchsorted(bounds, dist) % 2 == 0, 1, -1)
x = np.concatenate([-dist[::-1], dist])
pol = np.concatenate([pol_right[::-1], pol_right])
img = np.tile(pol, (80, 1))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.2),
                               gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]})
ax1.imshow(img, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r",
           extent=[x[0], x[-1], 0, 1], vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax1.axvline(0, color="black", lw=2)
ax1.text(0, 1.06, "ridge axis", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax1.set_yticks([])
ax1.set_title("Symmetric magnetic anomaly stripes", fontsize=11)

age = np.abs(x) / 25.0  # spreading rate ~25 km/Myr each side
ax2.plot(x, age, color="#4269d0", lw=2)
ax2.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax2.set_xlabel("distance from ridge (km)")
ax2.set_ylabel("age (Myr)")
ax2.set_xlim(x[0], x[-1])
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Part C — Beyond the static frame {#sec-part-c}

The static frame is left behind here — systems that move over time, figures whose whole point is animation, and the honest depiction of what is not known. Uncertainty is drawn rather than suppressed; where a form is genuinely animated, a print or HTML book shows it as one representative still or a short small-multiple sequence.

## C1. Dynamical systems, chaos, and emergence {#sec-unit-c1}

*After Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (1994).*

### 88 — Lotka–Volterra phase portrait {#sec-lotkavolterra}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@lotka1925elements] \
> **Domain:** predator–prey limit cycle  

Predator and prey abundances chase each other around a closed orbit rather than settling to a point, and plotting one against the other turns a pair of coupled rate equations into a family of nested loops. Lotka set out the equations in 1925 [@lotka1925elements]; each initial condition traces its own conserved cycle, and the inset time series shows the same motion as the out-of-phase peaks familiar from population records.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lotkavolterra
#| fig-cap: "Predator–prey phase portrait: closed orbits, with an inset time series."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

np.random.seed(0)

a, b, c, d = 1.0, 0.1, 1.5, 0.075

def lv(t, z):
    x, y = z
    return [a * x - b * x * y, -c * y + d * x * y]

t_span = (0, 40)
t_eval = np.linspace(*t_span, 4000)
colors = ["#4269d0", "#efb118", "#ff725c", "#6cc5b0"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for i, x0 in enumerate([10, 15, 20, 25]):
    sol = solve_ivp(lv, t_span, [x0, 5], t_eval=t_eval, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-8)
    ax.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[1], color=colors[i], lw=1.3)
ax.set_xlabel("prey  x")
ax.set_ylabel("predator  y")
ax.set_title("Lotka–Volterra phase portrait")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

axin = ax.inset_axes([0.56, 0.60, 0.40, 0.36])
sol = solve_ivp(lv, t_span, [20, 5], t_eval=t_eval, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-8)
axin.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], color="#4269d0", lw=1)
axin.plot(sol.t, sol.y[1], color="#ff725c", lw=1)
axin.set_xticks([])
axin.set_yticks([])
axin.set_title("time series", fontsize=7)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 89 — The strange attractor {#sec-attractor}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@lorenz1963deterministic] \
> **Domain:** deterministic chaos with structure  

A deterministic system with no noise can still be unpredictable, and its trajectory need not wander freely — it settles onto a set with fixed geometry that it never leaves and never repeats. Lorenz found this in a three-variable convection model in 1963 [@lorenz1963deterministic]; the x–z projection is the double-lobed butterfly whose two wings the state orbits in an order no forecast can pin down.

```{python}
#| label: fig-attractor
#| fig-cap: "The Lorenz attractor, x–z projection (σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

np.random.seed(0)

sigma, rho, beta = 10.0, 28.0, 8.0 / 3.0

def lorenz(t, s):
    x, y, z = s
    return [sigma * (y - x), x * (rho - z) - y, x * y - beta * z]

sol = solve_ivp(lorenz, (0, 60), [1.0, 1.0, 1.0],
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 60, 20000), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-9)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[2], color="#4269d0", lw=0.4)
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("z")
ax.set_title("The Lorenz attractor")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 90 — The bifurcation diagram {#sec-bifurcation}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@may1976simple] \
> **Domain:** the road to chaos  

Raising a single control parameter takes a system from one stable state, to an oscillation between two, then four, then a cascade of doublings that ends in chaos. May's 1976 review made the logistic map the emblem of this route [@may1976simple]; iterating x = r·x(1−x) and scattering the settled values against r draws the period-doubling tree with its self-similar windows of order inside the chaos.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bifurcation
#| fig-cap: "Logistic-map bifurcation diagram: attractor values versus growth rate r."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

rs = np.linspace(2.5, 4.0, 1400)
x = 1e-5 * np.ones_like(rs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for _ in range(600):          # discard transient
    x = rs * x * (1 - x)
for _ in range(300):          # plot the attractor
    x = rs * x * (1 - x)
    ax.plot(rs, x, ",k", alpha=0.25)

ax.set_xlabel("growth rate  r")
ax.set_ylabel("attractor  x")
ax.set_title("Logistic-map bifurcation diagram")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 91 — Double pendulum {#sec-doublependulum}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@shinbrot1992chaos] \
> **Domain:** sensitive dependence you can watch  

Two double pendulums released from all-but-identical angles keep step for a moment and then swing wildly apart, making sensitive dependence on initial conditions visible without any equations on the page. Shinbrot and colleagues used exactly this apparatus to demonstrate chaos in a table-top mechanical system [@shinbrot1992chaos]; the tip traces below start 0.01 radians apart and diverge within seconds. The physical form is animated — a single still stands in for the motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-doublependulum
#| fig-cap: "Two double-pendulum tip traces from near-identical starts, diverging."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

np.random.seed(0)

g, L1, L2, m1, m2 = 9.81, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0

def deriv(t, y):
    th1, w1, th2, w2 = y
    dth = th2 - th1
    den1 = (m1 + m2) * L1 - m2 * L1 * np.cos(dth) ** 2
    dw1 = (m2 * L1 * w1 ** 2 * np.sin(dth) * np.cos(dth)
           + m2 * g * np.sin(th2) * np.cos(dth)
           + m2 * L2 * w2 ** 2 * np.sin(dth)
           - (m1 + m2) * g * np.sin(th1)) / den1
    den2 = (L2 / L1) * den1
    dw2 = (-m2 * L2 * w2 ** 2 * np.sin(dth) * np.cos(dth)
           + (m1 + m2) * g * np.sin(th1) * np.cos(dth)
           - (m1 + m2) * L1 * w1 ** 2 * np.sin(dth)
           - (m1 + m2) * g * np.sin(th2)) / den2
    return [w1, dw1, w2, dw2]

t_eval = np.linspace(0, 20, 6000)

def tip(sol):
    th1, th2 = sol.y[0], sol.y[2]
    x = L1 * np.sin(th1) + L2 * np.sin(th2)
    y = -L1 * np.cos(th1) - L2 * np.cos(th2)
    return x, y

s1 = solve_ivp(deriv, (0, 20), [np.pi / 2, 0, np.pi / 2, 0],
               t_eval=t_eval, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-9)
s2 = solve_ivp(deriv, (0, 20), [np.pi / 2 + 1e-2, 0, np.pi / 2, 0],
               t_eval=t_eval, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-9)
x1, y1 = tip(s1)
x2, y2 = tip(s2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(x1, y1, color="#4269d0", lw=0.5, label="start θ")
ax.plot(x2, y2, color="#ff725c", lw=0.5, label="start θ + 0.01")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("Double pendulum — tip traces diverge")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 92 — The Mandelbrot set / fractal {#sec-mandelbrot}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@mandelbrot1982fractal] \
> **Domain:** self-similarity at every scale  

The boundary of the Mandelbrot set has detail at every magnification, an infinitely intricate coastline generated by iterating one quadratic map. Mandelbrot's 1982 book gave fractal geometry its name and this figure its icon [@mandelbrot1982fractal]; colouring each point c by how fast z = z² + c escapes to infinity draws the familiar bulbed body and its filigree edge.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mandelbrot
#| fig-cap: "The Mandelbrot set, coloured by escape-time iteration count."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

N = 500
x = np.linspace(-2.2, 0.8, N)
y = np.linspace(-1.3, 1.3, N)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
C = X + 1j * Y
Z = np.zeros_like(C)
counts = np.zeros(C.shape, dtype=int)
maxit = 80
alive = np.ones(C.shape, dtype=bool)

for i in range(maxit):
    Z[alive] = Z[alive] ** 2 + C[alive]
    escaped = np.abs(Z) > 2.0
    newly = escaped & alive
    counts[newly] = i
    alive &= ~escaped
counts[alive] = maxit

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.imshow(counts, extent=[-2.2, 0.8, -1.3, 1.3], cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
ax.set_xlabel("Re(c)")
ax.set_ylabel("Im(c)")
ax.set_title("The Mandelbrot set")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 93 — Reaction–diffusion (Turing) patterns {#sec-turing}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@turing1952chemical] \
> **Domain:** pattern self-organising  

Two chemicals that react and diffuse at different rates can break a uniform field into spots and stripes on their own, no template required. Turing proposed this mechanism for biological pattern in 1952 [@turing1952chemical]; a short Gray–Scott simulation started from a small seed self-organises into the maze of blobs shown here.

```{python}
#| label: fig-turing
#| fig-cap: "A Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion field self-organised into spots and stripes."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n = 120
U = np.ones((n, n))
V = np.zeros((n, n))
r = 10
c = n // 2
U[c - r:c + r, c - r:c + r] = 0.50
V[c - r:c + r, c - r:c + r] = 0.25
V += 0.02 * rng.random((n, n))

Du, Dv, f, k = 0.16, 0.08, 0.060, 0.062

def lap(Z):
    return (-4 * Z
            + np.roll(Z, 1, 0) + np.roll(Z, -1, 0)
            + np.roll(Z, 1, 1) + np.roll(Z, -1, 1))

for _ in range(4000):
    uvv = U * V * V
    U += Du * lap(U) - uvv + f * (1 - U)
    V += Dv * lap(V) + uvv - (f + k) * V

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.imshow(V, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Reaction–diffusion (Turing) pattern")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 94 — Flocking / boids {#sec-boids}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@reynolds1987flocks] \
> **Domain:** emergence from local rules  

Coherent flocking needs no leader and no global plan — three local rules, keep apart, match your neighbours' heading, steer toward their centre, are enough for a crowd to move as one. Reynolds introduced this model of "boids" in 1987 [@reynolds1987flocks]; after a few hundred steps the velocity arrows below have aligned into a common drift.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boids
#| fig-cap: "Boids after simulation: positions with velocity arrows aligned into a flock."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

N = 40
size = 20.0
pos = rng.uniform(0, size, (N, 2))
vel = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (N, 2))

def limit(v, m):
    s = np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    s[s == 0] = 1.0
    return v * np.minimum(s, m) / s

for _ in range(200):
    diff = pos[:, None, :] - pos[None, :, :]
    dist = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=2)
    np.fill_diagonal(dist, np.inf)
    coh = np.zeros((N, 2))
    ali = np.zeros((N, 2))
    sep = np.zeros((N, 2))
    for i in range(N):
        near = dist[i] < 5.0
        if near.any():
            coh[i] = pos[near].mean(0) - pos[i]
            ali[i] = vel[near].mean(0)
        close = dist[i] < 1.5
        if close.any():
            sep[i] = (pos[i] - pos[close]).sum(0)
    vel += 0.01 * coh + 0.05 * ali + 0.05 * sep
    vel = limit(vel, 1.0)
    pos = (pos + vel) % size

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.quiver(pos[:, 0], pos[:, 1], vel[:, 0], vel[:, 1],
          color="#4269d0", angles="xy")
ax.set_xlim(0, size)
ax.set_ylim(0, size)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("Flocking — local rules, one flock")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 95 — SIR epidemic curve {#sec-sir}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@kermack1927contribution] \
> **Domain:** contagion dynamics  

Splitting a population into susceptible, infective, and recovered compartments and letting infection flow between them produces the single-humped epidemic curve, with its peak and its burnt-out tail. Kermack and McKendrick set out the compartmental equations in 1927 [@kermack1927contribution]; the infective fraction rises, crests when the susceptible pool runs thin, and decays.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sir
#| fig-cap: "SIR compartments over time, with the classic infective peak."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

np.random.seed(0)

beta, gamma = 0.4, 0.1

def sir(t, y):
    S, I, R = y
    return [-beta * S * I, beta * S * I - gamma * I, gamma * I]

sol = solve_ivp(sir, (0, 160), [0.99, 0.01, 0.0],
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 160, 400))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], color="#4269d0", label="Susceptible")
ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[1], color="#ff725c", label="Infective")
ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[2], color="#3ca951", label="Recovered")
ax.set_xlabel("time (days)")
ax.set_ylabel("fraction of population")
ax.set_title("SIR epidemic curve")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## C2. Interaction, animation, and narrative {#sec-unit-c2}

*After Cairo, The Functional Art (2012).*

### 96 — Gapminder bubbles {#sec-gapminder}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@rosling2007visual] \
> **Domain:** wealth vs health vs time, animated  

Four variables ride on one scatter — income on a log x-axis, life expectancy on y, population as bubble area, region as colour — and running it across years turns development into visible motion. Rosling's Gapminder presentations made this the definitive animated statistical graphic [@rosling2007visual]; the frame below is one representative year, since the animation over time collapses to a single still in print.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gapminder
#| fig-cap: "Gapminder bubbles for one representative year (synthetic country data)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

regions = ["Africa", "Americas", "Asia", "Europe", "Oceania"]
colors = {"Africa": "#ff725c", "Americas": "#efb118", "Asia": "#4269d0",
          "Europe": "#6cc5b0", "Oceania": "#a463f2"}
counts = {"Africa": 12, "Americas": 8, "Asia": 14, "Europe": 10, "Oceania": 3}
base_income = {"Africa": 2000, "Americas": 9000, "Asia": 6000,
               "Europe": 25000, "Oceania": 20000}
base_life = {"Africa": 58, "Americas": 72, "Asia": 70,
             "Europe": 79, "Oceania": 78}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for reg in regions:
    nn = counts[reg]
    inc = base_income[reg] * np.exp(rng.normal(0, 0.5, nn))
    life = base_life[reg] + 4 * np.log(inc / base_income[reg]) + rng.normal(0, 2, nn)
    pop = 10 ** rng.uniform(6.5, 8.7, nn)
    ax.scatter(inc, life, s=pop / 3e4, color=colors[reg], alpha=0.6,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, label=reg)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("income per person (log)")
ax.set_ylabel("life expectancy (years)")
ax.set_title("Gapminder bubbles — one year")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 97 — Sequence alignment / genome browser {#sec-genomebrowser}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@kent2002human] \
> **Domain:** zoom from chromosome to base  

A genome browser stacks heterogeneous data on a shared coordinate axis — gene models, read coverage, conservation — so that any locus can be read across all tracks at once and zoomed from whole chromosome down to single base. Kent's UCSC browser fixed this track layout for genomics in 2002 [@kent2002human]; genes appear as exon boxes joined by intron lines above histogram and conservation tracks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-genomebrowser
#| fig-cap: "A genome-browser track view: genes, coverage, and conservation on one axis."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

L = 1000
xs = np.arange(L)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))

# coverage histogram track
cov = np.abs(np.convolve(rng.normal(0, 1, L), np.ones(30) / 30, mode="same"))
ax.fill_between(xs, 8, 8 + cov / cov.max() * 1.6, color="#4269d0", step="mid")
ax.text(-40, 8.8, "coverage", fontsize=7, ha="right", va="center")

# conservation track
cons = (np.sin(xs / 40) + 1) / 2 * rng.uniform(0.3, 1, L)
ax.fill_between(xs, 6, 6 + cons * 1.4, color="#6cc5b0")
ax.text(-40, 6.7, "conservation", fontsize=7, ha="right", va="center")

# gene tracks: exon boxes joined by an intron line
def draw_gene(y, exons):
    ax.plot([exons[0][0], exons[-1][1]], [y, y], color="0.3", lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    for a, b in exons:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((a, y - 0.25), b - a, 0.5, color="#efb118", zorder=2))

draw_gene(4, [(60, 110), (180, 230), (320, 360), (500, 560)])
draw_gene(3, [(400, 460), (620, 700), (820, 880)])
draw_gene(2, [(120, 160), (240, 300)])
ax.text(-40, 3, "genes", fontsize=7, ha="right", va="center")

ax.set_xlim(-120, L)
ax.set_ylim(1.5, 10)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("chromosome coordinate (bp)")
ax.set_title("Genome-browser track view")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 98 — Geologic time spiral / stratigraphic column {#sec-geotime}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@smith1815delineation] \
> **Domain:** deep time compressed  

A stratigraphic column stacks the eons and eras vertically with thickness scaled to duration, compressing four and a half billion years into a single legible strip that reads oldest at the bottom. William Smith's 1815 geological map established stratigraphic order as the organising principle of deep time [@smith1815delineation]; the column below colours each interval and sizes it by the span it covers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-geotime
#| fig-cap: "A stratigraphic column: eons and eras stacked, thickness scaled to duration."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

np.random.seed(0)

# (name, duration in Ma, colour)
layers = [
    ("Cenozoic", 66, "#efb118"),
    ("Mesozoic", 252 - 66, "#6cc5b0"),
    ("Paleozoic", 541 - 252, "#4269d0"),
    ("Proterozoic", 2500 - 541, "#a463f2"),
    ("Archean", 4000 - 2500, "#ff725c"),
    ("Hadean", 4600 - 4000, "#9c6b4e"),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 5.6))
bottom = 0
for name, dur, col in layers:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, bottom), 1, dur, color=col, ec="white"))
    ax.text(1.1, bottom + dur / 2, name, va="center", fontsize=9)
    bottom += dur

ax.set_ylim(0, bottom)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2.4)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_ylabel("age (Ma before present)")
ax.set_title("Stratigraphic column — deep time")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## C3. Encoding uncertainty — and reading wisely {#sec-unit-c3}

*After Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (2019), and Tufte on the honest depiction of uncertainty.*

### 99 — Confidence / credible intervals, error bars, fan charts {#sec-intervals}

> **Class:** shared genre idiom \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@neyman1937outline] \
> **Domain:** uncertainty made visible  

An estimate without its interval is half a statement; error bars and shaded bands attach the range of plausible values to every point and every fitted curve. Neyman's 1937 paper defined the confidence interval that these bars most often carry [@neyman1937outline]; a wide bar and a narrow one side by side say directly how much a number can be trusted.

```{python}
#| label: fig-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Point estimates with 95% error bars, and a fitted line with a shaded band."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.6))

groups = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]
means = np.array([5.2, 4.1, 6.0, 4.8, 5.5])
err = np.array([0.4, 0.9, 0.3, 1.2, 0.5])
ax1.errorbar(range(len(groups)), means, yerr=1.96 * err, fmt="o",
             color="#4269d0", ecolor="#4269d0", capsize=4)
ax1.set_xticks(range(len(groups)))
ax1.set_xticklabels(groups)
ax1.set_ylabel("estimate")
ax1.set_title("95% CIs by group", fontsize=9)
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 60)
y = 1.0 + 0.5 * x
band = 0.5 + 0.05 * np.abs(x - 5)
ax2.plot(x, y, color="#ff725c")
ax2.fill_between(x, y - 1.96 * band, y + 1.96 * band, color="#ff725c", alpha=0.25)
ax2.set_title("fitted line ± 95%", fontsize=9)
ax2.set_xlabel("x")
ax2.set_ylabel("y")
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 100 — Poll-of-polls fan chart {#sec-fanchart}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@britton1998inflation] \
> **Domain:** uncertainty as the message  

A fan chart puts uncertainty at the centre of the graphic: a central projection surrounded by nested predictive bands that fan wider the further ahead the forecast reaches. Britton, Fisher and Whitley described the Bank of England's inflation fan in 1998 [@britton1998inflation]; the darkening-to-lightening bands say plainly that the future is a distribution, not a line.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fanchart
#| fig-cap: "A fan chart: central projection with predictive bands widening ahead."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm

np.random.seed(0)

t_hist = np.arange(-12, 1)
hist = 2.0 + 0.1 * t_hist + 0.2 * np.sin(t_hist / 2)

t_fut = np.arange(0, 13)
central = hist[-1] + 0.05 * t_fut
sigma = 0.15 * np.sqrt(t_fut)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(t_hist, hist, color="0.2", lw=1.5)
for lvl in [0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3]:
    z = norm.ppf(0.5 + lvl / 2)
    ax.fill_between(t_fut, central - z * sigma, central + z * sigma,
                    color="#ff725c", alpha=0.18)
ax.plot(t_fut, central, color="#ff725c", lw=1.2)
ax.axvline(0, color="0.6", ls="--", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("quarters from now")
ax.set_ylabel("projected value (%)")
ax.set_title("Fan chart — widening ahead")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 101 — Bayesian updating {#sec-bayes}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@bayes1763essay] \
> **Domain:** prior to posterior  

Bayesian updating is one picture: a prior belief, multiplied by the likelihood of the data, renormalised into a posterior that is sharper than either. The rule traces to Bayes's essay published in 1763 [@bayes1763essay]; a Beta prior times a binomial likelihood gives a Beta posterior, and plotting all three on one axis shows belief concentrating as evidence arrives.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bayes
#| fig-cap: "Prior, likelihood, and posterior densities — the posterior sharpens."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import beta as beta_dist
from scipy.integrate import trapezoid

np.random.seed(0)

theta = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)
a0, b0 = 2, 2            # prior
n, k = 20, 14           # 14 successes out of 20

lik = theta ** k * (1 - theta) ** (n - k)
lik /= trapezoid(lik, theta)
prior = beta_dist.pdf(theta, a0, b0)
post = beta_dist.pdf(theta, a0 + k, b0 + n - k)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(theta, prior, color="#4269d0", label="prior  Beta(2, 2)")
ax.plot(theta, lik, color="#efb118", label="likelihood  (14/20)")
ax.plot(theta, post, color="#ff725c", label="posterior")
ax.fill_between(theta, post, color="#ff725c", alpha=0.15)
ax.set_xlabel("θ")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.set_title("Bayesian updating")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 102 — ROC curve + confusion matrix {#sec-roc}

> **Class:** named first \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@green1966signal] \
> **Domain:** decision under a threshold  

Any classifier that scores cases trades false alarms against missed hits as its threshold slides, and the ROC curve plots that whole trade-off while the confusion matrix pins down one chosen operating point. Green and Swets brought signal-detection theory and the ROC curve into psychophysics in 1966 [@green1966signal]; the area under the curve summarises separability, and the 2×2 grid counts the four outcomes at the threshold picked.

```{python}
#| label: fig-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve with AUC (left) and a confusion matrix at a chosen threshold (right)."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import trapezoid

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

neg = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 1000)
pos = rng.normal(1.5, 1.0, 1000)

thr = np.linspace(-4, 6, 300)
tpr = np.array([(pos >= t).mean() for t in thr])
fpr = np.array([(neg >= t).mean() for t in thr])
order = np.argsort(fpr)
auc = trapezoid(tpr[order], fpr[order])

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
ax1.plot(fpr, tpr, color="#4269d0", lw=1.6)
ax1.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="0.6", lw=0.8)
ax1.set_xlabel("false positive rate")
ax1.set_ylabel("true positive rate")
ax1.set_title(f"ROC  (AUC = {auc:.2f})", fontsize=9)
ax1.set_aspect("equal")

t0 = 0.75
TP = int((pos >= t0).sum())
FN = int((pos < t0).sum())
FP = int((neg >= t0).sum())
TN = int((neg < t0).sum())
cm = np.array([[TN, FP], [FN, TP]])
ax2.imshow(cm, cmap="viridis")
ax2.set_xticks([0, 1])
ax2.set_xticklabels(["pred −", "pred +"], fontsize=8)
ax2.set_yticks([0, 1])
ax2.set_yticklabels(["true −", "true +"], fontsize=8)
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2):
        ax2.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center",
                 color="white", fontsize=10)
ax2.set_title("confusion (θ = 0.75)", fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### 103 — Null distribution / permutation test {#sec-permutation}

> **Class:** canonical reference \
> **Canonical introduction:** [@fisher1935design] \
> **Domain:** what "significant" means  

A permutation test makes the null hypothesis concrete: shuffle the group labels many times, recompute the statistic each time, and the spread of those values is the distribution to beat. Fisher set out this logic of randomisation in 1935 [@fisher1935design]; marking the observed difference against the shuffled histogram turns the p-value into a visible tail fraction.

```{python}
#| label: fig-permutation
#| fig-cap: "A permutation null distribution with the observed statistic marked in the tail."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

a = rng.normal(0.5, 1.0, 30)
b = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 30)
obs = a.mean() - b.mean()

pooled = np.concatenate([a, b])
n = len(a)
null = np.empty(5000)
for i in range(5000):
    perm = rng.permutation(pooled)
    null[i] = perm[:n].mean() - perm[n:].mean()

pval = (np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.hist(null, bins=50, color="#6cc5b0", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(obs, color="#ff725c", lw=2, label=f"observed = {obs:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("mean difference under label shuffling")
ax.set_ylabel("count")
ax.set_title(f"Permutation null  (p = {pval:.3f})")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
